title: Was an orange ever a "norange"? | PORTMANTEAUS & WORD MASHUPS

entries.note: From French [[from:porter]], to carry, and [[from:manteau]], mantle; once a servant carrying a king's robes, now a bag; [[see:Lewis Carroll]] applied it to blended words.
Jess's own surname is a portmanteau, blending her maiden name Farris with her Greek husband's surname Zafiris.
Author of Alice's Adventures in Wonderland who coined [[see:portmanteau]] as a term for blended words in his introduction to The Hunting of the Snark.
Carroll's example of a portmanteau word, blending fuming and furious, said by someone with a perfectly balanced mind.
Comes directly from French [[from:manteau]], the coat element in [[same-root:portmanteau]].
[[see:Lewis Carroll]]'s poem from Through the Looking-Glass about a quest to slay the jabberwock, full of portmanteaus meant to be understood from their parts.
A [[see:Jabberwocky]] portmanteau of lithe and slimy that never caught on.
A blend of gallop and triumph that originated in [[see:Lewis Carroll]]'s work and is still used.
A blend of chuckle and snort from [[see:Lewis Carroll]]'s work, sandwiching one word inside the other, now in common usage.
Originally a combination of splash and spatter.
An 18th-century mashup of stow and cache.
A well-known food portmanteau of breakfast and lunch.
A Derby restaurant listed strawberry gateaux with the French plural X, so Rob's French wife complained of false advertising when only one cake came.
A portmanteau of hungry and angry.
A portmanteau of spoon and fork.
A mock cocktail, which Rob considers a very elegant portmanteau.
A rare three-way portmanteau: a deboned chicken inside a deboned duck inside a deboned turkey, assumed to be an American invention.
A Disneyland hot dog wrapped in a pickle, battered and deep-fried, cited as typical of American food combinations like the [[see:turducken]].
A food portmanteau of croissant and [[see:doughnut]] that Rob doubts was invented by the French.
Jess recalls the term being popularised in the US, perhaps New York, though inspired by European dishes; she hedges this.
JFK's line, supposedly meaning "I am a doughnut", though Berliners understood he meant a resident, since they call the doughnut [[see:Pfannkuchen]].
Name for a jam-filled doughnut across much of Germany but not in Berlin itself; also what Berlin residents call themselves.
Berlin's name for the jam doughnut called a [[see:Berliner (German)]] elsewhere, confusing to Rob since it is too round for a pancake.
Redrawing voting districts for advantage; blends [[from:Elbridge Gerry]]'s name with [[from:salamander]], after his convoluted 1812 district drawn as a dragon.
Massachusetts governor in 1812, later vice president under James Madison, whose convoluted district gave us [[gave:gerrymander]].
Meant a dragon-like fire beast before it named the real creature; it gave the second half of [[gave:gerrymander]].
An economics portmanteau Rob finds acceptable thanks to the shared "in" sound.
An economic slump combined with high inflation; Rob is unimpressed by it as a portmanteau.
Stagnant economy plus inflation; a poor portmanteau to Rob because stagnant and inflation share no overlapping letters.
Guess plus estimate; flows nicely, but corporate overuse has put Jess off it.
Chill plus relax, which Rob finds pointless since both parts mean the same thing.
Gigantic plus enormous, another redundant blend of near-synonyms.
Disaster plus catastrophe, used to stress something is really bad but saying the same thing twice.
One of the cuter portmanteaus, which the hosts say describes themselves.
Originally a portmanteau of electric and execute, first recorded in 1889 referring to electric-chair executions.
A technology portmanteau of breath and analyzer.
A modern portmanteau of friend and enemy.
A modern portmanteau of sex and texting.
Used in Germany for mixing German (Deutsch) and English.
A linguistics portmanteau for mixing Spanish and English, alongside [[see:Denglisch]] and [[see:Franglais]].
A portmanteau for mixing French and English.
Insinuating via innuendo; an early-20th-century favourite, quoted from Compton Mackenzie in 1921.
A Nissan Micra advertising campaign built on coined portmanteaus like [[see:spafe]], inspiring Rob's schoolfriends to coin their own.
Spacious plus safe, coined in the [[see:Do you speak Micra]] campaign; Jess finds it horrible.
Looks like an adjective with French -al but comes from Middle English [[from:bride ale]], a party for a bride; misinterpreted as an adjective.
A Middle English harvest party, an example of adding ale to make a party word, as in the source of [[see:bridal]].
A missing adjective for groom; Jess suggests groomal, groomulous or groomic as counterparts to [[see:bridal]].
When sounds shift between words that often appear together, like brackets moving, as with [[see:umpire]].
Middle English noumpere; through [[see:rebracketing]] the N moved to the article, so a noumpere became an umpire.
Splits as helico- plus -pter from Greek [[from:helix]], spiral, and [[from:pteron]], wing, meaning spiral wing, but copter gets rebracketed onto other words.
An example of -copter, rebracketed from [[see:helicopter]], tacked onto other words.
Means wing finger, sharing [[same-root:pteron]] with [[same-root:helicopter]]; its P was pronounced in Greek but silenced by English [[see:phonotactics]].
The rules of pronunciation; English dislikes P and T together at a word's start, hence silent P in [[see:pterodactyl]].
Originally a napron, from French; the N moved to the article; related to [[same-root:napkin]] and French [[same-root:nappe]].
Today's French word for tablecloth, showing the original N of [[same-root:apron]].
Literally a small tablecloth or nap, related to [[same-root:apron]].
The UK's only venomous snake; originally a nadder, still [[same-root:Natter]] in German.
The German word for [[same-root:adder]], keeping the original initial N.
The reverse of [[see:adder]]: an ewt took the N from the article to become a newt.
Originally an ekename, eke meaning additional; rebracketed, perhaps influenced by folk etymology from [[see:Nick]].
Swedish term with no initial N, matching the original form of [[same-root:nickname]].
Associated with the devil in idioms; a generic name like [[see:Jack]], also short for Nicholas; possibly behind the folk etymology of [[see:nickname]].
Like [[see:Nick]], a generic name that turns up in idioms.
Jess calls it devil's fart bread, Rob goblin fart, an example of devilish [[see:Nick]].
Middle English citations of nostrich instead of ostrich, a rebracketing that didn't survive into Modern English.
Apple was sometimes erroneously written napple, though the internet wrongly claims it should be napple.
Middle English examples of a negg for an egg, understandable among mostly illiterate people who only heard it.
Listed in Cawdrey's Table Alphabeticall for annoyance, but both forms already existed in Old French, so it may not be English rebracketing.
From Hamburg, a sandwich purportedly from there, rebracketed so -burger attaches to words like [[see:cheeseburger]].
Uses -burger rebracketed from [[see:hamburger]]; Rob jokes there is no German town of Cheeseburg.
Another word taking -burger rebracketed from [[see:hamburger]].
Cyber- is taken off it and used in words like [[see:cyberspace]], though the full Greek root would give cybern-.
Uses cyber- rebracketed from [[see:cybernetics]]; cybernspace would be more awkward.
Rebracketed so -holic is tacked onto words like [[see:workaholic]], though in [[from:alcohol]] the detachable part is Arabic [[see:al]].
Uses -holic rebracketed from [[see:alcoholic]].
At least partly Arabic-derived; its truly separable part is the Arabic article [[see:al]].
The Arabic definite article; a word starting with al- of unclear origin is probably Arabic.
Never a norange in English or French; from Sanskrit [[from:nāraṅga]] via Persian and Arabic, the N lost in Italian; colour named after the fruit.
The Spanish word with an initial N, which people cite against the claim that [[see:orange]] was never a norange.
What the French called the orange, fitting the idea that the fruit was named after the tree.
The French for potato, an example of fruits and vegetables once called apples, like the [[see:orange apple]].
Its D comes from Labrador, not poodle, so every later -doodle breed rebrackets that D from Labradoodle.
One of the many -doodle crosses taking the D rebracketed from [[see:Labradoodle]].
A true portmanteau dog name, a cross of pug and beagle.
Rob thinks it should be cockapoodle; Jess says it ends in -poo to sound like a bird.
A Shih Tzu–poodle cross whose -poo probably comes from [[see:cockapoo]] rather than poodle.
When letters or sounds swap places within a word, as in [[see:aks]] for ask.
Metathesis of ask in London and American dialects; Rob says it is not a survival of Old English axian but the same phenomenon recurring.
Jess's cousin's childhood metathesis of spaghetti, a cute example of what kids do.
A common metathesised pronunciation of comfortable, more natural in rhotic American accents.
Metathesis of pretty, which Jess says to her dog.
Originally brid, changed by metathesis.
Was waps in Old English; Rob's favourite Middle English form is wappes, which might make him hate them less.
Earlier thrid, spelled with the [[see:thorn]] letter, changed by metathesis.
The letter from Old and Middle English used to spell the early form of [[see:third]].
Pulled from [[from:universe]], where it meant turn, it now means world or realm, as in [[see:Buffyverse]] and [[see:metaverse]].
Literally turned into one, the verse part meaning one turn; source of the element [[gave:-verse]].
An example of [[see:-verse]] meaning world or realm.
An example of [[see:-verse]] meaning world or realm.
From [[see:Orson Scott Card]]'s Ender's Game universe, cited by some sources as the first extension of [[see:-verse]].
Ender's Game author credited by some sources with first extending [[see:-verse]], a claim Jess contests citing [[see:Multiverse]].
Coined by [[see:William James]] in the 1890s with the [[see:-verse]] element; multiple universes, an odd, oxymoronic compound.
Philosopher who coined [[see:Multiverse]] in the 1890s, predating [[see:Orson Scott Card]]'s use of [[see:-verse]].
